newsitem.title: USA: Maine Yankee in preliminary sale talks -officials.
newsitem.headline: Maine Yankee in preliminary sale talks -officials.

text.p: The utility owners of the troubled Maine Yankee nuclear power plant are negotiating a possible sale of the plant, officials said Wednesday.
Officials declined to release the name of the potential buyer for the 910-megawatt facility, but said the purchaser was interested in buying all the ownership shares.
"I would emphasis that discussions are very preliminary and it just isn't apropriate to amplify or provide additional details at this early stage," spokeswoman Maureen Brown said.

Maine Yankee is 38 percent owned by Central Maine Power Co, 20 percent each by New England Electric System and Northeast Utilities, 7 percent by Bangor Hydro, 5 percent by Maine Public Service Co. and 10 percent by other New England utilities.

Entergy Corp, which has been managing Maine Yankee's operations for the utility owners since February, is not the potential buyer, said Maine Yankee president Mike Sellman, who is also a vice president with Entergy.

Officials declined to say what price was being asked for the 25-year-old facility. Maine Yankee has an outstanding debt of $150 million, of which $88 million is related to original construction costs.
Brown said while there was no formal timetable for concluding the negotiations, plant officials hoped with about 30 days "to have some sense of direction these talks might head."
Maine Yankee has had a series of expensive safety related problems over the past two years and is on the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's "Watch List" of nuclear plants needing increased scrutiny.
The plant has been off-line since Dec. 6 to fix problems including misrouted electrical cables and is not expected to resume operation until late summer. The plant is licensed to operate until 2008.

Maine Yankee board chairman David Flanagan acknowledged in a writen statement Wednesday announcing the negotiations that some owners were concerned "about spending increases and their potential impact on long-term plant economics."
